means: The camera sits behind the subject and you see their back. A camera-position tag, not a description of body language.
does: Rebuilds the whole shot. You lose the face and every expression tag with it - brow, mouth, gaze and tears are all spent on pixels that are no longer in frame - and in exchange you gain the character's view of whatever they are facing. It also carries a downstream cost the still frame will not warn you about: the video model cannot turn a character around who is already facing away, and asking it to is what produces the warping people blame on the model. One vocabulary trap - if you want the face turned back over the shoulder, the tag is 'looking back', not this plus looking at viewer. And in the prose-dialect films the same words appear as ordinary English ('firing from behind an overturned pew'), where they mean something else entirely.
reach_for_it: an entrance, a character facing down what is in front of them, or withholding a face the audience wants to see
used_in: 28 uses across nine films - berserk, carriage-seven, chrono, derby, episode01, her-name, hollow-choir, hound and last-good-year - making it far the most-used tag in this set after the count tags. Exposed in the authoring layer as shot.facing back and back_three_quarter
example_base: 1boy, solo, male focus, short dark hair, plain jacket, standing, city street, daytime
read_it_as: Compare the SHADING, colour and line - not the pose or framing. Adding any clause re-rolls the model's conditioning, so composition moves between the two panels even at a fixed seed. An img2img pass from one fixed base image would isolate the tag properly; that is not built yet.
